title: Why China needs more income taxation
gist: PIIE authors argue China's trade surplus reflects excess private saving (worsened by the housing bust), not fiscal policy, and that China should shift its tax mix from consumption taxes toward a broader progressive personal income tax (only ~1.2% of GDP in 2025) to boost consumption, rebuild fiscal capacity, and prepare for AI and pension pressures. They add that US tariffs have had only modest effects on the US current account; cutting US fiscal deficits would work better.

themes.theme: China savings glut and trade imbalance

insights.claim: China's private consumption is only about 40 percent of GDP, far lower than in most countries, and weak domestic demand exacerbates its global trade surplus.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Low household consumption is the structural root of China's export push; watch consumption share as the key rebalancing gauge.
insights.quote: Private consumption in China is only 40 percent of GDP, far lower than in most countries.
insights.locator: Body: China's large current account surpluses

insights.claim: Even including government social transfers in kind of around 7 percent of GDP, China's private consumption still lags most major economies.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Adjusting for in-kind transfers does not explain away China's consumption gap; rebalancing thesis holds.
insights.locator: Notes 1

insights.claim: PIIE authors argue China's excess private saving stems from the housing bust, which sharply curtailed private investment without lowering the high household saving rate.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Housing bust keeps savings-investment gap wide, sustaining deflationary pressure and current account surpluses.
insights.quote: It has roots in the Chinese housing bust, which has sharply curtailed private investment without diminishing China's high private saving rate
insights.locator: What accounts for the excess of Chinese savings?

insights.claim: Falling Chinese house values, absent alternative savings options such as international investment, may push households to save more as property becomes a less reliable store of value.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Capital-account liberalization or new savings vehicles could matter for Chinese household behavior and outward flows.
insights.locator: Lower house values—especially without the availability

insights.claim: China's on-budget government deficits of more than 5 percent of GDP have not been enough to offset excess private savings or lift the economy convincingly out of deflationary pressures.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Fiscal stimulus alone is not reversing Chinese deflation; expect persistent disinflationary export pricing.
insights.locator: Unlike the United States, China does not have a fiscal situation

insights.claim: Including off-budget activity, China's fiscal deficit exceeded 12 percent of GDP in recent years by the IMF's augmented measure.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: China's true fiscal space is much tighter than headline numbers suggest.
insights.locator: Notes 2

insights.claim: Unlike the US, China's international imbalance is not caused by its fiscal position; it is a private-sector savings excess, so the fix is tax structure rather than a larger deficit.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Policy debates pushing China for more stimulus miss the point; watch tax-structure reforms instead.
insights.quote: While a larger fiscal deficit isn't called for, China should consider reforming its tax structure, including an expansion of its income tax, to discourage excess private saving.
insights.locator: Unlike the United States, China does not have a fiscal situation

insights.claim: International imbalances are macroeconomic phenomena: deficit countries spend more than they earn and borrow abroad, while surplus countries like China accumulate foreign assets and export excess production.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Trade balances follow savings-investment gaps, not tariff levels.
insights.locator: International imbalances have long been understood

insights.claim: The massive US tariffs of 2025–26 have had only modest effects on the US current account, so US trade wars should be expected to be ineffective at fixing the trade imbalance.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Don't expect tariffs to close the US current account deficit; dollar and external-financing dynamics persist.
insights.quote: Yet the massive US tariffs of 2025–26 have only had modest effects on the US current account.

insights.claim: Since 2020 the United States has accounted for more than half of the world's net current account deficits and has become the world's largest debtor.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: US remains dependent on foreign financing, a structural factor for Treasuries and the dollar.
insights.locator: For its part, the United States should expect

insights.claim: Reducing US fiscal deficits, recently averaging about 6 percent of GDP, would be far more effective than tariffs at cutting US national dissaving, but there is little political appetite for fiscal restraint.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Persistent ~6% deficits imply continued large current account deficits and heavy Treasury supply.
insights.quote: there appears to be little political appetite for fiscal restraint at present
insights.locator: For its part, the United States should expect

insights.claim: By end-2025 China's general government debt reached nearly 70 percent of GDP, or nearly 130 percent including off-budget debt, per the IMF.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Beijing's limited room to deficit-finance demand constrains big stimulus expectations.

insights.claim: China's tax revenue as a share of GDP peaked in 2012 and has fallen steeply, accelerated by tax and fee cuts since 2018 and deepened by the housing bust that began in 2021.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Eroding revenue base forces eventual tax increases; watch for reform announcements.
insights.locator: China's government understandably argues

insights.claim: Local-government land sales, China's principal non-tax revenue source, are unlikely to rebound after the housing bust, so with an aging population Beijing needs to raise taxes.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Local government financing stress persists; tax hikes rather than land revenue must fill the gap.
insights.quote: If anything, the Chinese government needs to raise taxes
insights.locator: China's government understandably argues

insights.claim: China's personal income tax was only about 1.2 percent of GDP in 2025, the lowest in the G20 except Saudi Arabia, while consumption taxes (VAT, excise, tariffs) were about 6 percent of GDP.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: China's tax mix structurally penalizes consumption — a lever for rebalancing.
insights.locator: In particular, China should look to reforming its tax structure

insights.claim: China's tax revenue was only 12.6 percent of GDP in 2025; including social security contributions the total burden was 20.4 percent in 2023, above only India, Indonesia, Mexico and Saudi Arabia in the G20.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: China's fiscal capacity is low for a near-advanced economy, limiting countercyclical firepower.
insights.locator: In particular, China should look to reforming its tax structure

insights.claim: Shifting China's tax burden from consumption to income would correct a tilt toward saving, because China's biggest tax levers exempt savings while a broad income tax does not.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: A tax-mix shift is a concrete mechanism to raise Chinese consumption and shrink the trade surplus.
insights.quote: China's biggest tax levers exempt savings from taxation; a broad income tax does not.
insights.locator: Second, by taxing income instead of consumption

insights.claim: Chinese officials say they want to spur consumption, but their consumption-tax-heavy system does the opposite.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Stated pro-consumption policy is undermined by tax design; judge Beijing on tax reform, not rhetoric.
insights.quote: Chinese government officials often say they want to spur consumption, but the structure of their tax system does the opposite
insights.locator: Second, by taxing income instead of consumption

insights.claim: A revenue-neutral swap of steeper income taxes for lighter consumption taxes would shift burden to richer, higher-saving households and let lower-income households, who consume more of their income, spend more.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Distributional tax reform could lift aggregate consumption — positive for Chinese consumer-facing sectors.
insights.locator: Alleviating overall tax collection burdens

insights.claim: Refundable tax credits such as EITCs could give lower-income Chinese households negative tax rates, supporting consumption, incentivizing formal work and building tax compliance and administrative capacity.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Watch for refundable-credit pilots as a signal of serious consumption policy.
insights.locator: Third, these changes would make China's tax system more progressive

insights.claim: More than 70 percent of Chinese income tax filers pay no personal income tax, and the 1 percent earning over 1 million RMB (about $150,000) pay over half of PIT, so the challenge is to broaden the base while keeping progressivity.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: China's income tax base is extremely narrow; broadening is the reform to watch.
insights.quote: The 1 percent of tax filers earning more than 1 million RMB (about $150,000) annually account for over half of the total personal income tax collected.
insights.locator: In the United States, about 40 percent of households

insights.claim: A broader progressive income tax would fall more heavily on richer regions, letting Beijing redistribute fiscal resources to poorer regions; enforcing PIT on wealthy individuals' offshore trust income is a first step against evasion and capital flight.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Tighter enforcement on offshore wealth signals stricter capital-flight controls for wealthy Chinese.
insights.locator: A broader, but still progressive, income tax

themes.theme: AI and pensions: future fiscal needs

insights.claim: Consumption and labor taxes both face base erosion if AI and robots displace labor, while a strong income tax including business taxes can reach AI winners via capital gains and corporate profits.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: AI-driven shift from labor to capital income implies future tax pressure on corporate profits and capital gains.
insights.quote: Consumption and labor taxes are both subject to tax base erosion if labor is displaced by AI and robots.
insights.locator: Fourth, a more meaningful income tax

insights.claim: China's pension system already relies on growing general-budget subsidies, and expanding the income tax may be the most feasible revenue source of the magnitude needed to fund aging-related pension needs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Pension underfunding is a long-run fiscal pressure that will force Chinese tax reform.
insights.quote: Redesigning and expanding China's income tax code may be the most feasible source of additional revenue
insights.locator: Fifth, and finally, China faces the long-term impact of aging

insights.claim: Alternative Chinese pension fixes look infeasible near-term: contribution rates are already among the highest internationally, replacement rates are below adequate levels, and retirement ages were only modestly raised in 2024.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Few levers besides tax revenue remain for Chinese pension funding.

insights.claim: The 2024 Third Plenum proposed income tax reform, but action has been slow and the measures so far are incremental.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Don't price fast Chinese tax reform; incrementalism is the base case.
insights.quote: action has been slow, and the measures suggested so far are relatively incremental

insights.claim: China is unlikely to institute a meaningful real estate property tax during the housing slump because it would accelerate price declines.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Tianlei Huang,Jacob Funk Kirkegaard
insights.so_what: Removes a tail risk for Chinese property prices near-term.
